_note: One-page summaries of the GHL lesson videos. Shown on lessons.html (and printable). 'for' is who should watch. 'watch' is the trimmed length in minutes.

lessons.title: Welcome, parent and athlete
points: Kids get hurt from imbalance, overtraining and untrained stabilizer muscles. This program fixes those three.
Athlete: thank your parent. This costs time and money and they did it for you.

lessons.title: How the training works (athlete)
points: You can do this without mom or dad.
The first week is slow because you are watching the demos. By week two you know them by name.
Nothing you do at practice trains your body like this. That is your edge.
do: Open the player and do the ten-minute first session today.

lessons.title: The Parent Playbook
points: Two jobs for you: know what is in the program and why, and keep her consistent.
Not every kid has the work ethic. That is not her fault and it does not mean she won't make it. Pushing is the parent's job.
When she doesn't want to: ask "What's your goal?" If it is still high school or college, then this is what it takes. You do it tired. You do it sore.
Say out loud that you push because it is her goal, not yours. The day it stops being her goal is the day you stop.
Make it automatic: same days and times every week, attached to something she already does.
do: Ask her what her goal is and write it down.
Pick the recurring days and times.
Set up this week in the planner together on Sunday night.

lessons.title: Why kids get hurt: the five reasons
points: Weak stabilizer muscles. The small muscles around the knee and ankle only get strong on purpose. The Stability workouts do that.
Weakness in joint positions. Games put her in bent, twisted positions her training never visits. Isometric holds and pulses teach her body to be strong there.
Tightness. More practice, no recovery. Mobility, stretching and rolling, and she learns to do them herself.
Muscle imbalances. Strong quads, weak hamstrings and glutes: where most ACL tears come from. The Foundation workouts load the back of the body.
Compensation. When something hurts, she moves differently and other muscles take over. That is when the real injury happens. Pain that lingers is a stop-and-check, never a play-through.
do: Agree with her: pain that lasts more than two days means we stop and get it looked at.

lessons.title: Recovery and mobility (parent)
points: More is not better. Extra training needs extra recovery or she gets hurt.
Never stack a hard workout and a training session in one day. If she does two things, put mobility or stretching between them.

lessons.title: Recovery and mobility (athlete)
points: Recovery doesn't feel like it does anything. That is why nobody does it, and why it is your edge.
Same days, same times, every week, attached to practice. No matter what.
do: Pick your recovery days on the week planner.

lessons.title: The five types of recovery
points: Myofascial release, stretching, cold plunge, mobility, and ice or heat (only if hurt).

lessons.title: Stretching
points: Dynamic stretches only. Holding a stretch 20 to 30 seconds switches the muscle off and can make you tighter.
Five stretches, then straight into the MAT holds.
do: Stretching workout in the player, after practice or on an off day.

lessons.title: MAT isometric holds
points: Stretching can switch a muscle off. Six holds, six reps of six seconds, right after stretching, switches them back on.
Two minutes. Nobody else teaches this.
Watch the MAT Test video once: Annabelle strong, stretched, weak, six holds, strong again.
do: MAT Holds in the player, every time after stretching, and before games.

lessons.title: Mobility
points: Tight joints mean a smaller range of motion, which means slower and less agile.
Five minutes before practice, or on the field while you wait for the coach, or while watching TV.
do: Mobility workout in the player, two or three times a week.

lessons.title: Myofascial release
points: A fancy word for massage. Tight muscles pull a joint out of line, and running on it like that is how you get hurt. Do not run through pain.
Knee pain usually comes from the inner quad and where the muscles insert at the knee. Roll those first.
Tools, all cheap: small foam roller, massage gun, hand roller, tennis or baseball. Pick the one you have.
do: Recovery page in the player: tick the spots you rolled.
Watch the four tool videos once each, then you won't need them.

lessons.title: Example schedule
points: Mobility before practice. Stretching and rolling after. Massage gun in the car on the way home.
Off days: ten minutes of mobility and stretching.
Game days: mobility before the team warm-up, recovery after.
do: The week planner does this for you. Tap your practice and game days.

lessons.title: The Youth Athlete Warm-Up
points: Team warm-ups don't wake up the muscles that protect you. Yours does, with one band, in the 15 minutes before the team starts.
Every game, no exceptions. Practices as often as you can.
Be the one who starts it. Your teammates will copy you.
do: Band in the bag. Warm-Up in the player before every game.

lessons.title: Balance and stability
points: Nobody trains the small muscles around the knee and ankle, or does single-leg work. These workouts do.
A Dyna Disc is enough. The BOSU is harder, not required.
Four exercises a workout, easiest to hardest. Stay on one as long as you like.
Off season twice a week. In season once.

lessons.title: Working the core
points: If you have the Core Edge, add one or two core exercises to a Stability or Foundation workout instead of a separate day.

lessons.title: The Foundation program
points: Strength, done in a balanced way: back of the body, glutes and hamstrings, core.
Body weight first. Add load slowly, off season.
In season, one strength workout a week at most. Off season is when you build.

lessons.title: Workout instructions
points: Eight workouts. One or two a week, four weeks each, then move on.
Short on time? Swap an exercise for a Stability one. The player has a button for it.
do: Foundation Workout 1 in the player. Work through the eight in order.

lessons.title: Example strength schedule
points: Off season: two strength workouts plus conditioning is plenty. The more work, the more recovery.
In season, no more than one strength workout a week, and only if she is doing her recovery. Stability, core, mobility and stretching carry the season.

faq._note: Drafted from Michelle's own words in the lesson transcripts. Items marked 'needs Michelle' have no answer in the videos yet.

items.q: She says her knee (or ankle, or back) hurts. What do we do?
items.a: Stop, don't play through it. Most knee pain in young athletes is tightness pulling the joint out of line, not an injury. Roll the inner quad near the knee, the hip flexors and the calves (Recovery page). If it is gone the next day, carry on. If it lingers more than two days, or there is swelling, that is a doctor visit, not a roll-it-out.

items.q: How old does she need to be?
items.a: The program is built for athletes roughly 8 to 16. Under 10, do it with her for the first few weeks. Michelle's own kids started this kind of work at 7 and 8.

items.q: Can she do strength work during the season?
items.a: Yes, but not more than one a week, and only if she is doing her recovery. The season is for stability, core, mobility and stretching. Off season and pre-season are when she builds strength.

Count her team sessions first. Four or more in a week: one workout. Two or three: two workouts, one Foundation and one Stability. Mobility two or three times, recovery two or three times, warm-up before every game. The week planner works this out when you tap her days.
A Dyna Disc does the job. The BOSU is harder, not required. Start with nothing but a mini band: the warm-up, mobility, stretching and MAT holds need no equipment.

items.q: She has a hard training session and a workout on the same day.
items.a: Don't. Move one. If two things must happen in one day, put mobility or stretching between them.
Holding a stretch for 20 to 30 seconds switches the muscle off and can make you tighter. Do the dynamic stretches in the program, then the MAT holds to switch the muscles back on.

items.q: She wears a knee brace. Can she do this?
She is hypermobile (very flexible). Anything different?
She is coming back from an injury.
